Weekly Sync: Usability Testing
Hi everyone,
Following the redesign in commit 7e49599, this week I’ll focus on testing the new flow with people who are unfamiliar with CKB.
I want to see whether newcomers can move through Journey, Cell Lab, Transaction Explorer, and Build & Test without extra guidance. I’ll note where they get stuck, which terms are unclear, and whether they understand how transaction inputs and outputs are handled.
Anyone new to CKB is welcome to try the live demo and share feedback in this thread.
I would also like to ask the committee to process my previous funding request for the work completed so far.

recent_posts.topic_title: CCC 2.0.0 Prerelease - CoBuild, Coin 和 CKBC(oin)
recent_posts.author: Hanssen
recent_posts.content_text:
本文不代表任何组织。同时发表在我的个人博客上。
我失败了。
从现在看，说不定我真的会像半年前担心的那样，等到明年才发布 CCC 2.0.0 版本。
「阅读 CCC 里 UDT 相关的工具。请帮我制定一份重写相关逻辑的方案。」
CCC Logo1512×567 80 KB
Coin
硬币的概念已经存在了上千年，在人类社会中承担着价值流通的职责。在 CKB 上，我们也有数字版本的硬币，即后来被称为 UDT 的寻常代币。每一枚硬币都由 CKB 上的一个 Cell 承载，由类型脚本约束着代表硬币面额的数据。一枚硬币可以拆分成多枚，多枚也可以组合回一枚，而每一枚又都可以在不同的地址中流通。
CKB 有两种货币资产，分别是原生代币和硬币。原生代币几乎是必须支持的类别，但处理原生代币相关的问题，例如最小占用费，却需要消耗开发者大量的心力。而当开发者终于准备支持硬币时，周边基础设施的缺失又让能完整支持硬币的生态应用少之又少，光是在链下实现简单的收付款就是一种挑战，更别说复杂的链上逻辑。
因此，在这次以硬币为主题的预发布里，我决定重写旧的 UDT 包，抛弃很多原来没设计好的部分。同时，我也决定用 Coin（硬币）这个旧名字代替不够直观的 UDT，因为它在社会中有着更广泛的共识，也更能直观体现 CKB 上寻常代币有着独立面额的特点。
CKBC(oin)
新的 Coin 包试图为应用简化硬币操作，而 CKBC(oin) 则试图将硬币的概念也拓展到原生代币上。对于只关心货币资产价值的应用，CKBC 的存在能让它们不再需要分别处理原生代币和硬币，从而降低应用的开发门槛。
在 CKBC(oin) 的设计中，用户必须通过锁定 CKB 才能铸造 CKBC，因此每一枚 CKBC 背后都对应着和面额相同数量的 CKB。锁定的 CKB 在链上以公共金库的形式存在，只有烧毁 CKBC 时才能解锁金库。
这种锁定并铸造的方案和 iCKB 很像。在两种设计中，用户都可以持有锁定了 CKB 价值的硬币。但在 iCKB 的设计中，CKB 被锁定在 Nervos DAO 中，以牺牲部分和 CKB 间的流动性为代价，为持有 iCKB 的用户提供了稳定的收益。
虽然 CKBC 和 iCKB 听起来会互相抢夺用户愿意锁定的 CKB，但它们绝非竞争关系。得益于 CKBC 和 CKB 间优良的流动性，用户随时可以解锁 CKBC 并重新锁定为 iCKB。CKBC 简单的设计帮开发者迈出了兼容硬币的第一步，而在这之后，他们只需要沿着同样的路径，就可以为已经支持了硬币标准的应用加入更多的硬币，包括 iCKB。
在 CKBC 的设计和工具包之后，我还完成了配套的网页工具。用户可以在网页上连接自己的钱包，完成 CKBC 的铸造、解锁和转账等操作。在实现这个工具的过程中，我也注意到了 CKBC 包里需要重新打磨的逻辑。
例如在设计中，CKBC 金库和 CKBC 代币其实是两种可以互相转换的硬币。比起要求开发者单独操作这两种硬币，最终实现利用了它们之间的强联系，让代币的铸造总随着 CKB 被锁定到金库中，而代币的烧毁也总随着金库被解锁。
再比如，CKBC 是去中心化的协议，所有人都共享同一套 CKBC 金库。如果只是简单按时间选择，那在多个用户同时操作时，多笔包含同一个金库的交易必然互相冲突。为了降低冲突发生的可能性，最终实现选用了基于概率选择金库的方式。
CKBC 网页工具1973×1126 180 KB
「这份设计中有几个明显的问题，请帮我评估可能的修复方案。」
命令行重新开始滚动，AI 继续搜索相关的资料。我有多长时间没好好写代码了呢？
对于觉得自己动手比给 AI 下指令更快的情况，我偶尔还会按自己的想法修改代码；难以用自然语言描述的构思，简短的伪代码也是不错的沟通方式；审阅 AI 生成的代码更是家常便饭，直到现在我也相信人类审核的必要性。
但我想说的不是这些。我已经记不得上一次认真思考解决问题的代码方案是什么时候了。我也忘了进入心流状态，几个小时盯着同一份代码是什么感觉。
把看到的问题粗暴地塞到对话框里，然后指派一个看着顺眼的方案；冲一杯咖啡，泡一杯茶，看会视频，刷会社交媒体，总之任何能打发 AI 思考时这段无聊时间的事情；别忘了时不时注意 AI 的进展，等着看它噼里啪啦地把结果吐出来。重复这个过程。
一阵烦躁。与其说我在意每个屏幕上各自切换着的内容，它们更像是思绪里的填充物，让我无暇在意自己在做的事情有多无聊。「迟早要被取代的家伙还在苟延残喘什么。」是啊，我在做什么？「也许我不该继续写代码。」也许我错得太久了。「再努力的人也只能沦为 AI 的训练数据。」人们怎么能这么心安理得？
我不愿让这些混乱的念头占领全部的空白。
「忘了之前对话的内容吧。有趣的想法：我想把 CKB 本身包装成代币，并从这个具体案例出发，重新思考我们需要怎样的工具。把提炼出来的概念叫做硬币 Coin，这样包装代币就可以叫 CKBCoin，你觉得怎么样？」
CoBuild
我签名释放了硬币，等量的硬币进入你的地址，这是一次最简单的硬币转账操作。但是，这个过程也可以理解成我烧毁了硬币，而你刚好铸造了等量的硬币，只看最终状态难以区分。
CKB 这种链上只关心最终状态转移的设计，的确减少了不必要的信息暴露，对隐私而言是件好事，但过程中的意图信息缺失也为开发者带来了额外的挑战。在交易组装、验证行为和数据统计等场景中，开发者们要不就得像个侦探一样，从最终结果反推出发生了什么事情；要不就提前做好小抄，额外记下交易的意图供后面参考。
为了存放意图数据，CoBuild 协议规定了一套统一的信息解析方式，从而在交易中开辟了额外的空间。除此之外，原始的 CoBuild 设计还包括了链上验证逻辑、应用间数据交换格式和可组合交易片段等规范。
不过，这次我在 CCC 中重新引入 CoBuild 协议，只是为了简化 Coin 包的操作。Spore 协议的教训，因过早在链上强制要求 CoBuild 信息而导致的开发体验灾难，至今难忘，我并不希望因为急于实现完整的 CoBuild 而重蹈覆辙。
在 CoBuild 包的帮助下，新的 Coin 包也保持了 CCC 一贯以来「交易流水线」的设计。在往交易里添加操作的过程中，工具可以通过 CoBuild 直接了解交易里已有的意图，避免潜在的冲突。因此，在同一笔交易中，开发者可以自由组合硬币的多种操作。
CoBuild 数据在交易中的位置2583×1053 174 KB
专业的用词、完整的解析、详细的描述……思想空洞，充满错误。
「请你对发布的内容负起责任，检查 AI 生成的内容。」
刚刚想要认真阅读的欣喜已经消失，心情从无奈变成了愤怒，又再次变回无奈。以为自己终于找回了故友赠予的礼物，却发现只是被随手丢弃的废物，被 AI 的长篇大论欺骗的我心里大概就是这样的感觉吧。
离新年还有四个月。
待办事项随着鼠标滚动，内容流出视野。我打从心底里知道，我该处理那些事情，给出没人会挑剔的正确答案，写下不批判任何人的文字，成为一个更聪明的 AI。
手指却在眼睛勇于看清最后一条内容前关闭了页面，但还是没能阻止堆积物透过鼻子攥住大脑。为什么我没在写代码？我该写代码了。我需要写代码了。我必须写代码了。
我想写代码了。
「回到之前的问题。调研 CoBuild 协议的设计，我想用它来记录交易构建过程中的意图。」

Hi zz_tovarishch,
Firstly I apologise for the time it took to respond .I wanted to complete the full rerun (transaction-count analysis and sensitivity analysis) and submit everything together, rather than send a half-baked response and follow up piecemeal.
I do appreciate the Committee’s scrutiny here and it has made the methodology and limitations of the current baseline substantially clearer than the original report did.
Correction to an earlier draft of this response, previously I stated “all 250 addresses have is_special = false.” That’s not accurate. Checking the actual retained data: is_special was never populated for the vast majority of addresses .
Only 13 of the 264 committed addresses have any retained value for it at all, and those are all null/unset, not confirmed false. There is no confirmed observation of is_special = true anywhere in the retained data, but “never observed true” and “confirmed false” are different claims, and I don’t want to overstate this.
1. Basis for the heuristic labels
is_special
The initial assumption behind is_special was that it could indicate an address performing automated or special-purpose activity that might behave differently from a normally operated human wallet.
More importantly: the code itself never lets is_special produce a bot_like label in the first place. It only appears as an exclusion condition on the human_like path (and not is_special).
So regardless of its actual values, it structurally cannot be the “alone” or “both” driver of any bot_like label under the current rule.
For the current dataset:
is_special alone: 0
Transaction-count threshold alone: 160
Both: 0
All 160 bot_like addresses were selected through the transaction-count threshold. I removed is_special from the labeling logic .This is because both it is not contributing to the current dataset and because it was never structurally able to.
Threshold basis
Current heuristic thresholds:
human_like: 1-50 lifetime transactions
bot_like: >=1,000 lifetime transactions
Addresses between these ranges: excluded
These are initial heuristic choices, not based on a formal CKB-specific study, known-identity dataset, or established research source. They’re being used as initial proxy-label boundaries, and the sensitivity analysis (§4) is the test of how robust the resulting labels and model are to changes in them.
2. Data collection and sampling
Command used:
python3 fetch_real_data.py --n-blocks 500 --max-per-pool 40 --max-tx-per-address 300 --out-dir data/real
Note: - - max-per-pool 40 caps each bucket at 40 addresses per invocation, enforced across runs via the resumable checkpoint .A single run of this exact command can’t produce the committed 160/104 split.
The command was run multiple times (resuming from checkpoint each time) to reach that total.
I don’t have the per-run parameter history to say how many invocations or whether --max-per-pool was ever changed. Flagging this rather than implying the single command above fully explains the dataset size.
Transaction-history lookback is capped at 200,000 transactions per address (–skip-tx-count-above, default), to reduce Explorer timeouts.
Returned transaction history is capped at 300 per wallet (–max-tx-per-address).
The classification query (/addresses/{address}) returns the lifetime transaction count as a single number, but the history endpoint used for feature extraction returns only a sample, capped at that 300.
This means:
Human-like wallets with <=50 lifetime transactions have their complete history represented within the 300-tx cap.
Bot-like wallets with >=1,000 lifetime transactions have only up to 300 transactions represented out of a much larger history.
We missed including the full transaction-count distribution and related statistics in the first training round .That round focused on extracting samples and training the baseline model, and this was overlooked. It’s being corrected in the current round: lifetime transaction counts, threshold distributions, class composition, label changes, and the sensitivity analysis are now included (§4).
3. Run-level provenance
The original data collection did not record run-level provenance . The commit hash, collection date, exact block range are not recorded, and I’m not reconstructing or estimating them retrospectively.
One clarification worth adding: The current version of fetch_real_data.py already contains a log_run_provenance() function that writes exactly this (timestamp, args, block range, git commit hash) to data/real/run_log.jsonl on every run, unconditionally.
Since no such file exists anywhere in the repo, either this logging was added to the script after the original collection ran, or it was present and the resulting log simply wasn’t committed.
I don’t have a way to determine which from what’s in the repo now, but it’s worth resolving .
If it’s the latter, the log may still be recoverable locally even though it isn’t in git.
No manual additions or removals were made to the dataset during the initial collection process. For the current rerun, collection parameters and provenance are being recorded explicitly (into run_log.jsonl) so the dataset going forward has a reproducible record.
4. Sensitivity / robustness analysis - complete
This is now done. Full results are committed to the repo as label_sensitivity_analysis.xlsx: ckb-intel/label_sensitivity_analysis.xlsx at main · FadhilMulinya/ckb-intel · GitHub (source: sensitivity_results.json, produced by sensitivity_analysis.py, which reuses train_eval.py’s model-selection/evaluation code directly rather than reimplementing it, so results are directly comparable to eval_results.json). Please see the linked spreadsheet directly for the full breakdown.
All 9 combinations of bot_min_tx in {500, 1,000, 2,000} x human_max_tx in {20, 50, 100} trained successfully.
Random Forest was selected in every case; held-out accuracy stayed in the 95.2%-100% range throughout.

Findings
Human-side labels drift over time, bot-side labels don’t.
At the current thresholds (1,000/50). Re-deriving labels from freshly-fetched lifetime tx_count drops 5 of the 91 originally-trained human_like addresses to excluded (none moved to bot_like).

Caveat .
The bot_min_tx = 500 rows are not evidence of robustness to a looser bot threshold. This analysis can only relabel addresses already in the 264-address committed pool, and every currently-labeled bot_like address in that pool already has tx_count >= 1,000 by construction.

5. Annotation guidelines and criteria
The current review uses the same heuristic framework used to construct the proxy labels (1-50 = human_like, >=1,000 = bot_like, excluded in between).
Wallet transaction history is then inspected to determine whether observed activity is broadly consistent with the assigned heuristic category.
There is no separate formal ground-truth definition of “human” or “bot,” and no formal “could not be determined” category - addresses outside the selected ranges are excluded rather than assigned an uncertain class.
This matches the code exactly: classify_address returns None for out-of-range addresses, and None-bucket addresses are never fetched or added to a pool.
6. Manual review and annotators
Two people: myself and wakoTheDev · GitHub, Paul wako is an experienced AI/ML engineer also contributing to this project.
We reviewed addresses separately, examining transaction histories against the heuristic categories.
Heuristic labels were visible during review , this is not a blind annotation process. Reviews were conducted separately but are not independent gold-standard annotations, since we both worked within the same heuristic framework.
No disagreements were formally recorded, no formal disagreement-resolution procedure was applied, and no inter-annotator agreement statistic was calculated, because this was not conducted as a formal independent annotation study.
7. Per-address review records
The original per-address annotation records were not retained as a contemporaneous dataset, and I’m not presenting a reconstruction as though it existed during the original review.
Ask: We can produce a new, structured per-address review table (address, initial heuristic label, manual review result, transaction-history evidence/reason) if explicitly required as part of the rerun .
8. Repository wording and the 95.24% result
The accurate description is: heuristic proxy labels, not verified ground truth. REPORT.md’s statement that all labels were manually verified is not accurate and is inconsistent with train_eval.py, the classifier README, and eval_results.json, all of which already use the correct language. I have corrected REPORT.md (§2.2, §2.3 compliance table, §7) to match.
The reported 95.24% accuracy is accuracy against the heuristic proxy labels , it is not verified accuracy for identifying human vs. automated wallet ownership. The manual wallet review is being treated as supporting inspection of transaction histories, not formal ground-truth verification.
9. Sampling limitations
Two, not one:
Transaction-window asymmetry. Human-like wallets (<=50 lifetime tx) have their complete history captured within the 300-tx return cap.
Bot-like wallets (>=1,000 lifetime tx) only ever have up to 300 transactions represented out of a much larger history.
Timing/interval features for bot-like wallets are therefore computed from a partial window, not full lifetime behavior.
Label decay over time (new - surfaced by the sensitivity analysis, §4): because tx_count only grows, the human_like/excluded boundary is not stable even at fixed thresholds.
A re-check today already shows ~5.5% of the trained human_like class (5/91) has drifted out of range since original collection.
Any future dataset refresh should expect a similar decay rate specifically in the human_like class, and the report should describe “91 human_like addresses” as a snapshot as of the original collection date, not a static property of those addresses going forward.
Both limitations are being explicitly considered when interpreting current model results and incorporated into the revised analysis.
The transaction-count analysis, sensitivity analysis, and per-address review table were not included in the first training round .A clear omission on our side, made when these provenance requirements weren’t yet defined.
This response and the attached files correct that gap. I appreciate the Committee’s scrutiny here. It has made the methodology and limitations of the current baseline substantially clearer than the original report did.
Best,
Fadhil

Relative to the on-chain tally discussion…
A focused request for technical review
The technical discussion in On-Chain Tally: DAO v1.1 Limits and a Deposit-Paired Voting Proposal (the thread is now closed) influenced several decisions in this project.
This is not presented as an alternative to DAO v1.1 or as a position on the governance disagreements in that thread. It is a separate testnet protocol. I want to explain where my implementation addresses the technical concerns raised there and get your honest reflection.
@phroi
Your stable-tally-input dilemma directly affected my design. Vote cells normally create two difficult choices: consume voter-locked cells and require every voter to sign, or reference them as cell deps and risk them being spent before aggregation.
I used governance-locked intent cells instead. A voter commits a choice into an immutable intent, but the governance script controls its valid transitions. An aggregator can consume it without the voter’s signature, while its exact refund owner remains committed separately in the intent data.
Your contention warning also changed the architecture. Voters no longer update one shared poll tally. They create independent intent cells, which are assigned to deterministic tally lanes. Different lanes can progress independently. Aggregators updating the same lane still contend for that lane cell, so the design partitions contention rather than eliminating it.
Each lane now stores a fixed sparse-Merkle root instead of a growing list of voter hashes. During aggregation, the contract verifies that each represented-voter key changes from absent to present under the authenticated input and output roots. The implementation is explained in Tally Lane Sparse-Merkle Implementation.
Two important limitations remain:
Finalization does not prove that every timely intent was aggregated.
Intent creation does not yet prove that one represented voter has only one live intent for a poll. Aggregation prevents double counting, but conflicting valid intents are resolved by whichever one is aggregated first.
The planned correction is a poll-scoped, one-shot authority consumed by either the direct voter or their delegate. I would value your view on whether governance-locked intents form a sound third path and whether that authority model preserves the property you obtained with VotingRightOwner without requiring DAO-deposit pairing.
@matt_ckb
Your concern about a centralized service being required to issue voter proofs was relevant when I introduced sparse-Merkle roots.
The structure here is different. Voters do not request or submit an SMT proof. They submit ordinary intent cells. A compiled proof is constructed only during aggregation from on-chain intent and marker state, and the contract verifies the resulting root transition.
The reference browser provider fails closed when its reconstructed state does not match the indexed lane root. No dedicated service has authority to issue voting proofs. RPC and indexer availability still affect discovery and frontend liveness, so I would appreciate scrutiny of whether this boundary is genuinely permissionless or whether I have only moved the operational dependency elsewhere.
@david-fi5box
Your three concerns were cell competition, transaction complexity, and migration of existing Nervos DAO deposits.
The current protocol addresses poll-wide cell competition structurally through independent vote intents and partitioned tally lanes. Same-lane aggregation remains serialized.
It avoids, but does not solve, the deposit-migration problem. Current polls are equal-weight and do not derive voting weight from Nervos DAO deposits. No existing DAO deposit must be withdrawn, re-locked, or adapted in Neuron for this version.
Weighted voting has been deferred. A future asset-weighted version would require a separately reviewed design.
You mentioned discussing cell-conflict approaches with the core team, developer relations, and other ecosystem developers. If any conclusions from those discussions are shareable, I would be grateful to compare them with this implementation.
Everything remains testnet-only and unaudited. I am specifically looking for adversarial review: where the design is unsound or where my assumption is too optimistic, or where I have missed something.

recent_posts.author: ebubedev
recent_posts.content_text:
Hey everyone,
Lightning is already huge. Millions of people, wallets, and merchants live there. Fiber is just getting started.
That gap is the real problem.
If Fiber only works inside Fiber, growth stays slow. If someone on Fiber can pay a Lightning invoice - and someone on Lightning can move value the other way - Fiber suddenly plugs into a network that already has users, habits, and demand.
That’s what a Cross-Chain Hub (CCH) is for.
In plain English: a CCH is a bridge between Fiber (Nervos) and Bitcoin Lightning. It swaps value between the two without a custodial middleman holding your money. You run the hub. You keep the keys.
Fiber already has the pieces for this. What’s hard is putting them together: Fiber node, Lightning node, CCH, keys, configs, Docker, funding, channels… It’s a lot. Easy to stall before you ever see a swap.
So I built Fiber CCH Hub - a standalone kit that turns “I want to run a hub” into something you can actually do.
Repo: GitHub - chukwuma619/fiber-cch-hub · GitHub
Why this matters for Nervos / Fiber
Fiber doesn’t need to beat Lightning on day one. It needs a bridge into Lightning’s world.
When hubs are easy to run:
Fiber users can pay into Lightning’s existing economy
Operators can provide liquidity between the two networks
Builders can experiment with real cross-network payments, not just demos inside one chain
More hubs → more routes → more usefulness → more reason to use Fiber.
This repo is meant to lower the barrier for that first step.
What you get
One stack:
Fiber (CKB testnet)
LND (Bitcoin testnet Lightning)
Standalone CCH wired between them
Scripts for keys, startup, and health checks
You create your own keys up front. Nothing is hidden behind a hosted service that holds your funds.
Run it
git clone https://github.com/chukwuma619/fiber-cch-hub.git
cd fiber-cch-hub
cp .env.example .env
make create-keys # save your Lightning seed
./start.sh

recent_posts.content_text:
Hi @Carl! I’m Hanssen from the Spark Committee. It’s great to see your exploration of the Fiber token swap. I have a few questions about the current proposal:
As you explained to @fgh earlier, users must unlock their RGB++ assets from the RGB++ Lock (from the BTC Leap back to CKB) before entering this swap. Does this mean the project isn’t very closely tied to RGB++?
Carl:
Right — a cell can’t carry both locks, so the design was never planning to keep the RGB++ lock alive inside the channel.
You mentioned that this project will create a new message type on top of Fiber’s gossip layer. Does this mean you need to modify the Fiber node? Will all users of this project need to use this modified node version?
Carl:
Advertisement layer — a new SwapAdvertisement message type carrying the asset pair being offered, the rate and fee, the operator’s public key, a signature over the message, and an expiry timestamp so stale offers don’t linger indefinitely. This rides Fiber’s existing peer gossip layer — the same broadcast/refresh mechanism already used today for node and channel announcements — deliberately, so this project isn’t introducing a new network transport or a new class of infrastructure to run and secure. A listening node simply gains the ability to also recognize and index this new message type.
Honestly, the current proposal deliverables focus too much on implementation details, and I can’t quite see what the final architecture of this project will look like. It would be great if you could provide more information on this point.

recent_posts.author: Carl
recent_posts.content_text:
Q1 — Does this mean the project isn’t closely tied to RGB++?
Not less tied — the leap step is the RGB++ integration, not a workaround of it. The unlock is a one-time technical necessity: a cell can’t carry both the RGB++ lock and a channel lock at once, so the asset has to leap out of RGB++'s lock before it can enter a channel. But every asset in this swap originates as an RGB++ asset — without RGB++, there’s nothing to advertise or swap. It’s the foundation, not a side door.
Q2 — Do you need to modify the Fiber node? Will all users need the modified version?
Nodes that want to broadcast or index swap advertisements need the extended fiber node — this isn’t a config toggle on stock Fiber, it’s a new message type added to the core gossip code. Regular unmodified nodes are unaffected and continue operating normally; they simply don’t participate in advertisement relay, the same way they wouldn’t relay any message type they don’t know about. This isn’t a hard fork of network consensus — it’s the same pattern Fiber already uses for CCH (cross-chain hub) forwarding today, which only works between CCH-aware nodes.
Q3 — The proposal is too implementation-heavy, what’s the final architecture?
Fair — that’s on me for leading with implementation. At a high level: an orchestration layer sits on top of the existing Actix backend, split into three pieces — a leap module (wraps RGB++'s own leap tooling, doesn’t reimplement it), an advertisement module (the new gossip message type above), and a swap execution module (generalizes CCH’s existing HTLC lock-and-reveal to a new asset pair). Chain interfaces underneath talk to Bitcoin and CKB directly. Nothing here is a new subsystem — three extensions wired into code that already works. I’ve got a full diagram and phase-by-phase build plan if that’s useful context.

From current mocked scaffold to a real, working leap-and-swap on testnet
This is the engineering plan behind the Spark proposal, written at implementation depth rather than grant-pitch depth. It assumes the current state of oxdev6/Fiber-RGB-Swap: an Actix backend and Yew frontend with working API endpoints (initiate, status, list), but simulated funding/leap logic and mock transaction hashes.
1. Full Architecture

│ - NEW: leap orchestration │

│ │ │ Module │ │ Module │
│ Wraps RGB++'s │ │ │ │ │
│ existing leap tx │ │ SwapAdvertisement │ │ Generalized CCH HTLC │
│ construction │ │ message: sign, │ │ lock-and-reveal, │
│ (rgbpp-sdk / ckb-cli│ │ broadcast, verify, │ │ parametrized over │
│ rgbpp tooling) │ │ index — a new │ │ asset type instead of │
│ │ │ gossip message │ │ hard-coded BTC pair │
│ │ │ type; requires the │ │ │
│ │ │ extended node to │ │ │
│ │ │ send/relay/index │ │ │
└──────────┬──────────┘ └─────────┬──────────┘ └────────────┬─────────────┘
│ │ │
▼ ▼ ▼
┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Chain Interfaces │
│ Bitcoin RPC/wallet (rust-bitcoin) CKB RPC (ckb-sdk-rust) │
│ — reads/spends RGB++ single-use-seal — cell queries, tx build, │
│ UTXOs tx send, Fiber node RPC │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Design principle carried through every layer: extend existing, proven code (Fiber’s gossip layer, CCH’s HTLC logic, RGB++'s leap tx construction) rather than reimplementing any of it. The only genuinely new code is the advertisement message type/index and the orchestration that chains leap → swap into one atomic-feeling user action.
Node compatibility note: the advertisement module adds a new message type to Fiber’s core gossip protocol (BroadcastMessage/GossipMessage in fiber-lib), not an already-recognized format. That means only nodes running this project’s extended fiber build can broadcast, relay, or index advertisements. Unmodified Fiber nodes are unaffected and keep operating normally — they just don’t participate in advertisement relay, the same way they don’t participate in CCH swaps unless running CCH-aware code today. This isn’t a network-wide upgrade or a hard fork; it’s opt-in, following the pattern CCH itself already set.
2. Step-by-Step Build Plan
Phase 0 — Environment and tooling (before writing new logic)
Stand up a CKB testnet node and a Fiber testnet node (fnn) locally; confirm you can query both via RPC.
Set up a Bitcoin testnet/signet wallet with test coins, and confirm you can construct and broadcast a basic transaction.
Pull in rgbpp-sdk (or the CLI tooling the RGB++ team ships, if the SDK isn’t stable enough) and get a single leap transaction working manually, outside your app, using their examples. Do not write your own leap logic until you’ve seen theirs work — this de-risks the entire project’s riskiest dependency first.
Add core Rust dependencies to the existing Actix backend: ckb-sdk-rust (CKB RPC/tx construction), rust-bitcoin (Bitcoin-side tx handling), whatever crate rgbpp-sdk exposes, and molecule if you need to hand-construct any CKB transaction fields not covered by the SDK.
Exit criterion: you can, from the command line, leap a real testnet RGB++ asset into a UDT, manually, using existing tooling. This is the single highest-risk unknown in the whole project — resolve it before building anything on top of it.
Phase 1 — Replace mock funding/leap logic with the real leap module
Wrap the manual leap flow from Phase 0 into a Rust module (leap.rs) with a clean interface: leap_to_udt(asset_ref, amount) -> Result<LeapReceipt>.
LeapReceipt should carry both transaction references (Bitcoin-side and CKB-side) so they’re available for the “How to Verify” step later — don’t discard them.

Repository: Akane-CN/spark-verify
Requested funding: $1,000, paid in CKB
Timeline: 6 weeks
1. Project overview
Spark Verify is an open source command-line tool and a small verify.toml format for CKB projects.
A project author describes a local devnet flow and the results that should be observed, such as whether a transaction commits or is rejected, which Cells exist after the run, whether a balance changed as expected, and how many CKB-VM cycles a script used. A reviewer runs one command and receives a pass/fail result with a structured evidence report.
The goal is to make the “How to Verify” section of a CKB project easier to run and repeat. Spark Verify will use the existing CKB development stack rather than replace it.
2. Team profile
Applicant and maintainer: Akane
GitHub: Akane-CN
Nervos Talk: Akane
Email: akane@random-walk.co.jp
3. Project background
CKB projects already have good tools for individual layers:
OffCKB provides a local development chain, development accounts, and script deployment.
CCC builds and signs CKB transactions.
ckb-debugger reports script errors and cycle usage.
ckb-testtool supports script-level tests.
The final acceptance check is still different for every project. Reviewers often have to follow repository-specific instructions, run several commands in the correct order, inspect RPC responses, and decide whether the observed result matches the project’s claims. These instructions become harder to repeat when tool versions or setup details change.
Spark Verify addresses this acceptance layer. It gives project authors a small CKB-specific vocabulary for declaring observable results and gives reviewers a consistent way to run those checks.
4. Solution
A participating project adds a verify.toml file and, where necessary, a small script that builds a signed CKB transaction.
Spark Verify will:
validate the manifest;
start a fresh local OffCKB devnet with pinned tool versions;
run the project’s declared steps;
submit transaction artifacts and record committed or rejected results;
check Cells, balances, script errors, and cycle limits; and
produce a JSON report and a readable terminal summary.
The first version will support local development chains only. It will not use testnet or mainnet private keys. Repository commands remain trusted project code, so the documentation will tell reviewers to run the tool only in an isolated environment without production secrets.
5. Technical approach
The CLI will be written in TypeScript and run with Bun. The repository will pin the Bun version and commit its Bun lockfile. The finished CLI will be published as an installable command-line package.
The implementation will include:
strict TOML parsing and runtime schema validation;
exact Bun, CKB, OffCKB, and ckb-debugger version checks;
OffCKB startup, readiness checks, development accounts, script resolution, and cleanup;
runner-owned submission of signed CCC-compatible transactions;
assertions for transaction status, script error groups, cycle limits, live Cells, capacity, Cell data, CKB balances, and UDT-compatible balances;
JSON reports containing the observed results and relevant environment information; and
a GitHub Action example for repositories that want to run the same checks in CI.
The report will distinguish the observed outcome from the environment used to produce it. This makes version or repository changes visible without claiming that arbitrary project code is formally deterministic.
6. Execution plan
Weeks 1-2: manifest and execution core
finalize the v0.1 manifest fields and schema;
implement manifest validation;
start and stop a pinned OffCKB environment;
execute project commands and submit signed transactions; and
cover both committed and script-rejected transaction examples.
Weeks 3-4: assertions and evidence reports
implement transaction, script-error, cycle, Cell, and balance checks;
produce JSON and terminal reports;
record repository, toolchain, genesis, and deployed-script information; and
add valid, invalid, passing, and failing test fixtures.
Week 5: CI and project example
publish a GitHub Action example;
adapt one CKB project to verify.toml; and
test clean-checkout verification on Ubuntu and macOS.
Week 6: release and documentation
publish the CLI package and tagged v0.1 specification;
complete the author guide and security notes;
record a short end-to-end demo; and
publish the Spark completion and budget report.
7. Required funding and breakdown
Total requested: $1,000, paid in CKB.
Manifest, schema, and initial execution work: $200
OffCKB execution adapter and transaction protocol: $300
Assertion engine and failure reporting: $250
Evidence report and GitHub Action: $150
Project example, release documentation, and demo: $100
No funding is requested for hosting or a web interface.
8. Deliverables and verification
Deliverables:
A versioned verify.toml v0.1 specification and machine-readable schema.
A published Bun-based spark-verify CLI package.
Conformance fixtures covering valid, invalid, passing, failing, committed, and rejected cases.
JSON evidence reports and readable terminal output.
A GitHub Action example.
A toy CKB example and one adapted CKB project.
Documentation, a demo, and a completion report.
A reviewer will be able to verify the release from a clean checkout:
git clone https://github.com/Akane-CN/spark-verify.git
cd spark-verify
bun install --frozen-lockfile
bun test
bun run build
bun run verify:release
The release check will demonstrate:
a successful transaction and matching Cell or balance result;
an intentionally failing claim with an expected-versus-observed diff;
a script-rejected transaction with its error evidence;
repeated runs with comparable reports; and
a visible failure or warning when the declared tool versions do not match.
